title: ECS200 Research Methods in Ecology
text:
Welcome
All workshop materials are provided in the GitHub repository ECS200, and the contents were developed by Nicholas Wu and Alethea Rea.
The ECS200 - Research Methods in Ecology workshops go through the steps of a typical research project, which look something like Figure 1.
First, you must import your data into R (Introduction to R). This usually means loading data stored in a file into a data frame in R. If you can’t get your data into R, you can’t analyse it!
Once your data are imported, check their quality (Week 1) and tidy them (Week 2). Tidying means putting the data into a consistent format where each column is a variable and each row is an observation. This makes analysis far easier: you can focus on answering questions rather than reformatting data for each new task.
Next, you will often transform your data (Week 2): for example, keeping observations from one site, creating new variables (e.g. speed from distance and time) or calculating summaries (e.g. counts or averages). Together, tidying and transforming are called wrangling, because getting data into a usable form can feel like a fight!
Once you have tidy, relevant data, you will use two main tools: visualisation and modelling. They complement each other, and most analyses move back and forth between them.
The final step is communication. Even the best model or figure is useless unless you can explain your findings clearly to others.
Surrounding all of these is programming. You will use code at every step. You don’t need to be an expert programmer, but better coding skills will help you work faster and solve problems more easily.

title: ECS200 Research Methods in Ecology
text:
How the workshops work
Each workshop is 2 hours plut 1 hour extra time. Spend about the first hour working through the page (reading, running the code and doing the 🧪 exercises), and the second hour on the assessment. Each assessment is an R script template that you download, complete and submit before the end of class.






Note



The optional workshops (time series, spatial data and movement data) are not assessed, but provide extra practice if you want to work with environmental, occupancy or movement data.

title: ECS200 Research Methods in Ecology
text:
Unit learning objectives
At the end of the unit, students should be able to:

Design ecological research using appropriate sampling strategies and analytical methods.
Apply appropriate statistical methods to test ecological hypotheses.
Apply R programming to process, analyse and visualise ecological datasets to professional standards.
Critically evaluate the strengths and limitations of research designs under different ecological conditions.
Communicate the findings of ecological research to professional standards.







ImportantImportant



When using R, make sure your code works on both your personal laptop and the Murdoch desktops. The mid-semester test will ONLY use Murdoch desktops (no laptops allowed). The R practicals and your research report can be done on your personal laptop or on the Murdoch desktops.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Before we start
Before the first workshop in Week 1, you need to be familiar with R, RStudio and the basics of coding. Work through this page before class. It takes about an hour.
Skip this step if R and RStudio are already installed on your computer.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Objects


Code
# Number of frogs counted at a pond
frogs <- 18

# Add 5 frogs observed the next day
frogs_total <- frogs + 5

# Print the result
frogs_total


[1] 23


<- is the assignment operator: it stores the value on the right in an object with the name on the left (object_name <- value). The object then appears in the Environment panel.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Vectors
A vector is a list of values of the same type, created with c() (for “combine”):


Code
# Leaf lengths (cm) of 5 eucalypt trees
leaf_sizes <- c(23.4, 21.8, 25.1, 19.7, 22.5)

# Average leaf size
mean(leaf_sizes)


[1] 22.5


mean() is a function. Functions take inputs (arguments) inside the brackets and return a result.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Data frames
A data frame is a table with rows (observations) and columns (variables). It is the object you will use most often in this unit.


Code
# A small data frame of species and their body mass (g)
example_data <- data.frame(
  species = c("Lizard", "Bird", "Bat"),
  mass    = c(15, 120, 35)
)

example_data


  species mass
1  Lizard   15
2    Bird  120
3     Bat   35

title: Introduction to R
section: Common problems and how to fix them
text:
Common problems and how to fix them
Click through the tabs. Each one shows an error you are likely to meet, why it happens and how to fix it.

Object not foundCould not find functionStuck with a +Unexpected symbolAnswer is NANumbers read as textColumn not foundggplot + in the wrong place


mean(leaf_size)
#> Error: object 'leaf_size' not found
Why: R cannot find an object with that name. Either it is spelt differently (leaf_sizes, Leaf_sizes), or the line that creates it was never run.
Fix: check the name in the Environment panel and copy it exactly. If it is not there, run the line that creates it (leaf_sizes <- c(...)) first. After you restart RStudio, run your script again from the top.
mean(leaf_sizes)  # correct name, created earlier


plant_calcium_data <- read_csv("data/plant_calcium.csv")
#> Error in read_csv(...) : could not find function "read_csv"
Why: the function belongs to a package that has not been loaded, or the function name is misspelt (Read_csv, read.csv vs read_csv).
Fix: run library(tidyverse) at the top of the script, or write the package name in front: readr::read_csv(). If you see there is no package called …, install it first with install.packages("package-name").


mean(c(23.4, 21.8, 25.1)
+
Why: the Console shows + instead of > when R thinks your command is not finished. Usually a bracket ) or a quotation mark " is missing.
Fix: press Esc in the Console to cancel, add the missing bracket or quote in your script, then run the line again. RStudio highlights the matching bracket when you click next to one, which helps you check pairs.
mean(c(23.4, 21.8, 25.1))  # two opening and two closing brackets


leaf_sizes <- c(23.4 21.8 25.1)
#> Error: unexpected numeric constant in "leaf_sizes <- c(23.4 21.8"
Why: something is missing between two values or words, most often a comma. Other causes are a space in an object name (leaf sizes) or a curly quote (“data”) pasted from Word or a PDF.
Fix: look at the spot R points to. Add the comma, use underscores instead of spaces in names, and retype any quotation marks in RStudio.
leaf_sizes <- c(23.4, 21.8, 25.1)


masses <- c(15, 120, NA, 35)
mean(masses)
#> [1] NA
Why: one value is missing (NA). R does not know the missing value, so it cannot know the mean either.
Fix: tell the function to ignore missing values with na.rm = TRUE. Also ask why the value is missing; you will deal with this properly in Week 1.
mean(masses, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] 56.66667


mean(plant_calcium_data$leaf_dry_mass)
#> Warning: argument is not numeric or logical: returning NA
Why: the column was imported as text (<chr>), usually because the spreadsheet had a word, a unit or a stray symbol in a number column (e.g. "12 g", "n/a", "<0.1").
Fix: check the column type with dplyr::glimpse(). Find the odd values with unique(plant_calcium_data$leaf_dry_mass), correct them in the raw data (or in R), then convert the column with as.numeric().


plant_calcium_data %>% dplyr::select(Watershed)
#> Error: Can't select columns that don't exist.
#> ✖ Column `Watershed` doesn't exist.
Why: column names are case-sensitive and must match exactly. Spreadsheet column names often contain spaces or capitals you did not notice.
Fix: print the exact names with names(plant_calcium_data) and copy them. If a name has a space, wrap it in backticks (`leaf mass`), or rename the column to something simple such as leaf_mass.


ggplot2::ggplot(example_data, ggplot2::aes(x = species, y = mass))
  + ggplot2::geom_col()
#> Error: Cannot use `+` with a single argument.
Why: each line of a ggplot must end with +. If + starts the next line, R thinks the first line is already a complete command.
Fix: move the + to the end of the line. (The same applies to the pipe %>% in Week 2.)
ggplot2::ggplot(example_data, ggplot2::aes(x = species, y = mass)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col()









TipStill stuck?




Read the error message slowly. It usually names the object, function or line that caused the problem.
Run your code one line at a time to find the line that breaks.
Copy the error message into a search engine. Someone has almost certainly had the same problem.
Type ?function_name (e.g. ?mean) in the Console to read its help page and examples.
Ask a classmate or your demonstrator, and show them the code and the error.





Exercise
🧪 Why does this code not work?


Code
my_variable <- 10
my_varıable
#> Error: object 'my_varıable' not found


Look carefully! Training your eyes to spot tiny differences pays off when coding.


Show answer

The second line uses a dotless “ı” instead of “i” in my_varıable, so R looks for an object that does not exist.

title: 1  Quality Check
text:
Background
Week 1: Quality checks and data exploration
In this workshop you will learn how to check the quality of raw data after you import it into R, and how to fix common errors. Workshop materials are available in the GitHub repository ECS200.
How do we know the data are ready for analysis? Before any analysis, check the raw data for the following:
These checks make sure your data are reliable and suitable for analysis, and they make you a trustworthy researcher.

title: 1  Quality Check
text:
Data structure and types: is each column the type you expect (number, category, text, date)? Use str() or dplyr::glimpse().
Missing values: where are they, and how many? Use colSums(is.na()) or visdat::vis_miss().
Duplicates: are any rows accidentally entered twice?
Categorical variables: are categories spelt consistently (e.g. “Male”, “male” and “M” are three different categories to R)?
Outliers or impossible values: negative lengths, a 50 kg frog, a date in the future.
Column names: meaningful, with no spaces or special characters.
Extra rows or columns: notes, totals or empty columns copied from a spreadsheet.

title: 1  Quality Check
text:
The tidyverse
In this unit we use the tidyverse style of coding. The tidyverse is a collection of R packages for importing, cleaning, transforming and plotting data that share the same grammar, so once you learn one package the others feel familiar. It is widely used in ecology because ecological data are often large and messy, collected across space and time, and have replicates nested within sites.

PipesTidy data


The pipe operator %>% passes the result of one step into the next step. Read it as “and then”.


Code
data %>%     # start with your data, and then...
  step_1() %>%  # do the first thing, and then...
  step_2()      # do the second thing

# Without pipes you read from the inside out
mean(log(c(1, 10, 100)))

# With pipes you read from top to bottom
c(1, 10, 100) %>%
  log() %>%
  mean()


Pipes make ecological workflows easier to read, because analyses usually involve several steps: import data, filter sites, remove missing values, calculate summaries, plot results.






Note



You may also see the “native” pipe |>. It does the same job. We use %>% in this unit because you will see it in most online help.




The tidyverse works best when the data look like this:


Each row is one observation.
Each column is one variable.
Each cell is one value.

The way you record data in the field is often different from the way R needs it. For example, if you measured seedling height in a factorial experiment with warming and fertiliser treatments, your field sheet might look like this:

You know how your experiment is set up, but R doesn’t! With eight measurements per row (all treatments and species for one block), R cannot tell which column is which treatment. In tidy format, each measurement gets its own row and each treatment gets its own column:

This is called long format. Now R can split the data by treatment, species or block. You will learn how to convert between formats in Week 2.


Code
# A small example of tidy data made with the data.frame() function
example_data <- data.frame(
  site        = c("A", "A", "B", "B"),
  species     = c("Skink", "Agamid", "Skink", "Frog"),
  temperature = c(28, 31, 26, 22),
  abundance   = c(5, 2, 8, 4)
)

example_data


  site species temperature abundance
1    A   Skink          28         5
2    A  Agamid          31         2
3    B   Skink          26         8
4    B    Frog          22         4

1.1. Initial check
First, check that every variable was imported as the right type. Common problems include:

Incorrect data types: a numeric column is read as text (chr) because it contains a symbol, a word, a comma instead of a decimal point, or an empty string.
Inconsistent coding: one category spelt several ways (“Male”, “male”, “M”), which R treats as different categories.
Header issues: a missing header row, or extra rows of notes at the top or bottom of the file.
Encoding problems: special characters (e.g. °, µ, accents) that display incorrectly.
Trailing spaces: “site A” and “site A” are different to R.

title: 1  Quality Check
text:
1.2. Identify missing values
Missing data can appear as blank cells, “NA”, “.”, “-” or other placeholders. If they are not handled properly, they cause errors or misleading results.



Code
# Count the missing values in each column
colSums(is.na(plant_calcium_data))


               year           watershed           elevation            transect 
                  0                   0                 119                   0 
             sample         stem_length           leaf1area           leaf2area 
                  0                   0                 126                 117 
      leaf_dry_mass       stem_dry_mass corrected_leaf_area 
                  0                   0                 119 


visdat::vis_dat() shows the whole data frame at once, coloured by the type of each column, with missing values in grey. visdat::vis_miss() shows only whether values are missing, and the percentage missing in each column.


Code
visdat::vis_dat(plant_calcium_data)









Code
visdat::vis_miss(plant_calcium_data)









What should you do with missing values? It depends on which columns they are in and on your question. tidyr::drop_na() removes rows with missing values:


Code
# Removes every row that has an NA in ANY column. Usually too harsh: here it
# would remove all of 2004, because elevation was not recorded that year.
plant_data_all_complete <- plant_calcium_data %>%
  tidyr::drop_na()

# Removes rows with an NA in the leaf2area column only. Use this when you are
# about to analyse leaf2area.
plant_data_clean <- plant_calcium_data %>%
  tidyr::drop_na(leaf2area)

# Compare the number of rows
nrow(plant_calcium_data)


[1] 359


Code
nrow(plant_data_all_complete)


[1] 233


Code
nrow(plant_data_clean)


[1] 242


Only remove missing values from the columns you actually need. Remember that a missing value (NA) is not the same as a zero. See Research Design.

  tidyr::drop_na(species_4)

# Check that the NAs have gone
visdat::vis_miss(fake_data_clean)

title: 1  Quality Check
text:
1.3. Checking duplicates

There are two kinds of duplicates:

Row duplicates: two rows are identical in every column. This is almost always an error (e.g. copy and paste) and should be removed.



Code
# Number of rows that are exact copies of an earlier row
sum(duplicated(plant_calcium_data))


[1] 0


Code
# Show the duplicated rows (none here, so this returns an empty table)
plant_calcium_data[duplicated(plant_calcium_data), ]


# A tibble: 0 × 11
# ℹ 11 variables: year <dbl>, watershed <chr>, elevation <chr>, transect <chr>,
#   sample <dbl>, stem_length <dbl>, leaf1area <dbl>, leaf2area <dbl>,
#   leaf_dry_mass <dbl>, stem_dry_mass <dbl>, corrected_leaf_area <dbl>


There are no duplicated rows in plant_calcium_data.

Value duplicates: the same value appears more than once in a column. This is usually real (e.g. two seedlings with a leaf mass of 0.03 g, especially after rounding). Be suspicious if there is a pattern, e.g. 2, 2, 6, 1, 2, 2, 9, 4, 2, 2, which suggests values were copied into the next row by accident. You, the researcher, have to decide whether duplicated values are real.



Code
# Number of values in leaf_dry_mass that repeat an earlier value
sum(duplicated(plant_calcium_data$leaf_dry_mass))


[1] 51


There are 51 repeated values in leaf_dry_mass, which is expected for masses rounded to four decimal places.

Remove it, either in Excel (easy) or with dplyr::distinct() (challenge).

  dplyr::distinct()

# Repeated values within each column (common for counts, so probably real)

sum(duplicated(fake_data$species_3))

title: 1  Quality Check
text:
2.1. Check for outliers
Outliers are not automatically “bad”, but they can cause problems. They can:

Distort results: a single extreme value can drag the mean, inflate the variation, and change the slope of a regression line.
Hide patterns: one extreme value squashes the rest of the data on a plot.
Reveal errors: data entry mistakes (typing 1000 instead of 100), faulty equipment, or mixed-up units (metres and centimetres).

Two simple plots will reveal most outliers.

BoxplotHistogram


ggplot2::geom_boxplot() draws a boxplot. Points beyond the whiskers are potential outliers (more than 1.5 × the interquartile range from the box).


Code
# Boxplot of leaf2area to look for potential outliers

2.2. Are the data normally distributed?
Many statistical tests (t-tests, ANOVA, linear regression) assume that the data (or, more precisely, the model’s residuals) are roughly normally distributed, with constant variance. If the data are strongly skewed, have outliers or have unequal variances, those tests can give biased estimates and wrong conclusions. You will learn how to check this properly in Weeks 5 and 7, and how to transform data in Week 2.

Background

Raw data are rarely in exactly the form you need. Usually you need to keep some rows, drop some columns, calculate new variables, summarise by group or change the layout of the table. In this workshop you will learn the dplyr and tidyr functions that handle almost all of these jobs, and how to write code that other people (including future you) can read. Workshop materials are available in the GitHub repository ECS200.
Five key dplyr functions (verbs) solve most data manipulation problems:
All of them can be combined with dplyr::group_by(), which makes the next function work group by group (e.g. one mean per watershed instead of one overall mean).

title: 4  Diversity Indices
text:
Background
Week 4: Measuring abundance, richness and diversity
How many individuals are there? How many species? How evenly are individuals spread among those species? In this workshop you will calculate the most common measures of abundance, species richness and diversity from survey data. These skills are essential for field-based projects and for jobs in ecological consulting and monitoring. Workshop materials are available in the GitHub repository ECS200.
Biodiversity has two main components: richness (how many species) and evenness (how equally individuals are spread among the species). Different metrics capture different combinations of these.
Other measures, such as alpha, beta and gamma diversity (diversity within a site, between sites and across a region) and taxonomic diversity, can be calculated with the vegan package.
Use the app to see how richness and evenness change the Shannon and Simpson indices.

title: 5  Statistical Inference
text:
Study context
Lizards are ectotherms, so their body temperature, and therefore how fast they can run, depends on the temperature around them. Performance usually increases with temperature up to an optimum and then drops off quickly (a thermal performance curve). Populations from hotter places often have a higher optimum.
To test this, 72 adult dragons were collected from a coastal (mild) and an inland (hot) population. In the lab, each lizard was randomly assigned to one test temperature (20, 28 or 36 °C), warmed to that temperature, and raced once along a 1 m racetrack to measure its maximum sprint speed (m/s). Each lizard was used only once, so every row is an independent lizard.



A mountain heath dragon (Rankinia diemensis).




Code
# Load the data
lizard_data <- readr::read_csv("data/lizard_sprint.csv")

# Check the structure: temperature is stored as a number, but in this
# experiment it is a treatment group, so we convert it to a factor.
lizard_data <- lizard_data %>%
  dplyr::mutate(temperature = factor(temperature, levels = c(20, 28, 36)),
                population  = factor(population))

dplyr::glimpse(lizard_data)


Rows: 72
Columns: 5
$ lizard_id    <chr> "L01", "L02", "L03", "L04", "L05", "L06", "L07", "L08", "…
$ population   <fct> inland, coastal, coastal, coastal, inland, coastal, coast…
$ temperature  <fct> 36, 28, 28, 28, 28, 36, 20, 20, 20, 20, 36, 28, 36, 36, 2…
$ mass_g       <dbl> 13.5, 16.1, 10.1, 10.1, 12.3, 10.9, 12.5, 12.4, 12.4, 14.…
$ sprint_speed <dbl> 1.60, 1.53, 1.81, 1.92, 1.44, 1.92, 0.95, 1.49, 1.09, 1.2…




Which test do I use?
All three tests ask the same question: is the difference between group means bigger than we would expect from random variation alone? They differ only in how many groups and how many predictors you have.









Research question
Predictor(s)
Test
R function




Do two groups differ?
1 categorical variable with 2 levels
Two-sample t-test
t.test()


Do three or more groups differ?
1 categorical variable with 3+ levels
One-way ANOVA
aov()


Do two factors affect the response, and does the effect of one depend on the other?
2 categorical variables
Two-way ANOVA
aov(y ~ A * B)









Note



Functions without a package name in front, such as t.test(), aov() and lm(), come with R itself (the stats package), so you never need to install or load them.

3. Check assumptions








Assumption
How to check
Here




Independence: each observation is from a different, unrelated unit
Think about the study design
✅ Each lizard was raced once at one temperature.


Normality: the data in each group are roughly bell-shaped
Histogram or Q-Q plot for each group
✅ See below.


Equal variances (only for the classic t-test)
Compare the SDs. If the largest SD is less than 2 × the smallest, they are similar enough
✅ Similar SDs, and Welch’s test does not need this anyway.

ggplot2::ggplot(lizard_two, ggplot2::aes(sample = sprint_speed)) +
  ggplot2::stat_qq() +
  ggplot2::stat_qq_line() +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ temperature) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "Sprint speed (m/s)") +
  ggplot2::theme_classic()















WarningWhen is a t-test NOT appropriate? (click to expand)













What you see
Why it is a problem
What to do instead




Strongly skewed data or big outliers, especially with small samples
The mean is pulled around by extreme values
Log-transform the response (Week 2), or use the non-parametric Wilcoxon rank-sum test, wilcox.test(y ~ group, data = ...)


The same individuals measured twice (before/after, left/right)
Observations are not independent
Paired t-test, t.test(before, after, paired = TRUE), or a mixed model (Week 12)


The response is a count (e.g. number of seedlings) with many zeros
Counts are not normally distributed
Generalised linear model for counts (Week 8)


The response is yes/no (e.g. alive/dead)
Not a continuous measurement
Logistic regression (Week 11)


More than two groups
Running many t-tests inflates false positives
One-way ANOVA (Part B)



For example, the Wilcoxon test compares the ranks of the values instead of the values themselves, so a single extreme value has little influence:


Code
wilcox.test(sprint_speed ~ temperature, data = lizard_two)



    Wilcoxon rank sum exact test

W = 25.5, p-value = 6.085e-10
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0

text:
4. Model
The formula response ~ group reads “sprint speed explained by temperature”.


Code
# Welch two-sample t-test (two-sided)
lizard_ttest <- t.test(sprint_speed ~ temperature, data = lizard_two)
lizard_ttest



    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  sprint_speed by temperature
t = -8.3763, df = 44.412, p-value = 1.088e-10
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group 20 and group 28 is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.7515599 -0.4601067
sample estimates:
mean in group 20 mean in group 28

title: 5  Statistical Inference
text:
5. Interpret

The output gives everything you need:

t = ...: the t value. Its sign only tells you which group was first alphabetically.
df = ...: degrees of freedom (Welch’s test gives a decimal value).
p-value = ...: the probability of seeing a difference this large if the null hypothesis were true.
95 percent confidence interval: the likely range for the true difference in means (group 1 minus group 2). If it does not include 0, the difference is significant at α = 0.05.
sample estimates: the mean of each group.

Lizards sprinted faster at 28 °C (mean ± SD = 1.82 ± 0.27 m/s) than at 20 °C (1.21 ± 0.23 m/s), an average increase of 0.61 m/s (95% CI 0.46 to 0.75 m/s; Welch’s t44.4 = 8.38, p < 0.001; Fig. 1).

title: 5  Statistical Inference
text:
3. Check assumptions
The assumptions are the same as for the t-test (independence, normality and equal variances), but for ANOVA we check them on the residuals. A residual is the distance between an observation and its group mean, the part of the data the model cannot explain.
The performance::check_model() function draws the main diagnostic plots, and each panel has a subtitle telling you what a “good” plot looks like.


Code
# Fit the one-way ANOVA first, then check its residuals
lizard_aov <- aov(sprint_speed ~ temperature, data = lizard_data)

performance::check_model(lizard_aov, check = c("homogeneity", "qq"))

















Assumption
Plot
Here

Homogeneity of variance: the reference line should be flat and horizontal
✅ Roughly flat.


Normal residuals
Normality of residuals: dots should fall along the line
✅ Dots follow the line.


Independence
Study design
✅ One lizard per measurement.

What you see
What to do instead




Very unequal spread among groups (largest SD > 2 × smallest)
Welch’s ANOVA, oneway.test(y ~ group, data = ...), which does not assume equal variances


Strongly skewed data or outliers with small samples
Log-transform, or the non-parametric Kruskal–Wallis test, kruskal.test(y ~ group, data = ...)


Repeated measurements on the same individuals or sites
Mixed-effects model (Week 12)


Counts or yes/no responses
Generalised linear models (Weeks 8 and 11)


A numeric predictor (e.g. temperature measured as 18.2, 22.7, 25.1 °C…)
Linear regression (Week 7)

Reading the output:

Lizards were 0.61 m/s faster at 28 °C than at 20 °C (95% CI 0.43–0.78, Tukey p < 0.001) and 0.58 m/s faster at 36 °C than at 20 °C (p < 0.001), but speed at 28 °C and 36 °C did not differ (difference = -0.02 m/s, p = 0.95).

title: 5  Statistical Inference
text:
3. Check assumptions
The assumptions are the same as for the one-way ANOVA. Fit the model first, then check the residuals.


Code
# Two-way ANOVA with interaction. temperature * population is shorthand for
# temperature + population + temperature:population
lizard_aov2 <- aov(sprint_speed ~ temperature * population, data = lizard_data)

performance::check_model(lizard_aov2, check = c("homogeneity", "qq"))









Both plots look fine and every lizard was tested only once, so the assumptions are met.






WarningWhen is a two-way ANOVA NOT appropriate? (click to expand)






Very unequal sample sizes among the combinations, or missing combinations: the order of terms then changes the results. Keep designs balanced where possible (see Research Design).
A numeric predictor (e.g. body mass) as well as a factor: use a linear model with both (Week 7).
Repeated measures, e.g. the same lizard raced at all three temperatures: observations from one lizard are not independent, so use a mixed-effects model with lizard as a random effect (Week 12).
Counts or yes/no responses: use generalised linear models (Weeks 8 and 11).

text:
5. Interpret
Always read the interaction row first. If the interaction is significant, the main effects can be misleading on their own. Here the main effect of population is not significant, yet the populations clearly respond differently to temperature.
Results sentence:

The effect of temperature on sprint speed depended on population (two-way ANOVA, temperature × population: F2,66 = 6.18, p = 0.003; Fig. 3). Coastal lizards were fastest at 28 °C and slowed down at 36 °C, whereas inland lizards continued to increase their speed up to 36 °C. Averaged over populations, speed increased with temperature (F2,66 = 51.48, p < 0.001), and there was no overall difference between populations (F1,66 = 0.01, p = 0.932). This is consistent with inland lizards having a higher thermal optimum.

Dates and times with lubridate
Week 6 (study week): Cleaning and plotting time series data
This is an optional tutorial for anyone working with data collected over time: repeated surveys, data loggers, weather records or growth measurements.
You will learn how to:
Most examples use datasets from the lterdatasampler package.
When you import a CSV file, dates are often read as text (chr). R needs to know they are dates before it can sort, plot or subtract them. The lubridate functions are named after the order of the parts in your dates: ymd() for year-month-day, dmy() for day-month-year, mdy() for month-day-year, with _hm or _hms added when there is a time.
Code
lubridate::dmy("05-01-1987")              # day-month-year


[1] "1987-01-05"


Code

[1] "1987-01-05"


Code

stream_dates <- lterdatasampler::luq_streamchem %>%

section: A worked example: cleaning a raw logger file
text:
A worked example: cleaning a raw logger file
Other common problems with microclimate loggers are outliers, duplicate times/values and missing data points. logger_bad.csv is a (simulated) week of hourly air temperature from a logger placed in a tree hollow. It contains all of these problems, just like a real file straight off a logger.
 logger_bad.csv


Code
logger_raw <- readr::read_csv("data/logger_bad.csv") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(date_time = lubridate::dmy_hm(date_time)) # text to date-time

summary(logger_raw)


   date_time                      air_temp     
 Min.   :2023-07-10 00:00:00   Min.   : 4.900  
 1st Qu.:2023-07-11 17:15:00   1st Qu.: 7.475  
 Median :2023-07-13 04:30:00   Median :11.650  
 Mean   :2023-07-13 09:56:23   Mean   :11.877  
 3rd Qu.:2023-07-15 05:45:00   3rd Qu.:15.825  
 Max.   :2023-07-16 23:00:00   Max.   :47.300  
                               NAs    :2       


Code
# Always plot the raw data first
ggplot2::ggplot(logger_raw, ggplot2::aes(x = date_time, y = air_temp)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line() +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "Air temperature (°C)") +
  ggplot2::theme_bw()









The plot already shows a spike to over 45 °C and a gap where the line jumps across missing hours. The other problems are hidden, so we check for each one.

1. Duplicates2. Outliers3. Missing data


Duplicates in logger files usually happen when the logger is downloaded twice and the files are joined (the same rows twice), or when the logger records two readings at the same time.
Exact duplicate rows are found and removed exactly as in Week 1 (section 1.3), with duplicated() and dplyr::distinct():


Code
sum(duplicated(logger_raw))   # number of rows that are exact copies


[1] 6


Code
logger_clean <- logger_raw %>%
  dplyr::distinct()           # keep one copy of each row


Duplicate times with different values are specific to time series. The rows are not identical, so dplyr::distinct() does not catch them, but a logger can only have one reading per time. Count the readings at each time:


Code
# Times that have more than one reading
logger_clean %>%
  dplyr::count(date_time) %>%
  dplyr::filter(n > 1)


# A tibble: 1 × 2
  date_time               n
  <dttm>              <int>
1 2023-07-12 06:00:00     2


Code
# Look at the readings at that time
logger_clean %>%
  dplyr::filter(date_time == lubridate::ymd_hm("2023-07-12 06:00"))


# A tibble: 2 × 2
  date_time           air_temp
  <dttm>                 <dbl>
1 2023-07-12 06:00:00      7.5
2 2023-07-12 06:00:00      8.3


Decide which reading to keep. If you cannot tell which one is right, take the mean of the readings at that time:


Code
logger_clean <- logger_clean %>%
  dplyr::group_by(date_time) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(air_temp = mean(air_temp), .groups = "drop") # one row per time

# Check: should now return no rows
logger_clean %>% dplyr::count(date_time) %>% dplyr::filter(n > 1)


# A tibble: 0 × 2
# ℹ 2 variables: date_time <dttm>, n <int>




The IQR rule from Week 1 looks at all values together. In a time series, a value can be within the normal range for the whole week but still be impossible for that time (e.g. 20 °C at 3 am on a night when it was 8 °C an hour earlier). Two time-series checks work better:

a physical limit: values outside what is possible at the site;
a rate of change: air temperature cannot jump by more than a few degrees in one hour, so compare each reading to the one before it with dplyr::lag().



Code
logger_clean <- logger_clean %>%
  dplyr::mutate(change = air_temp - dplyr::lag(air_temp)) # change since the last reading (°C)

# Readings above 40 °C, or that jumped more than 5 °C in an hour
logger_clean %>%
  dplyr::filter(air_temp > 40 | abs(change) > 5)


# A tibble: 3 × 3
  date_time           air_temp change
  <dttm>                 <dbl>  <dbl>
1 2023-07-13 14:00:00     47.3   31.4
2 2023-07-13 15:00:00     16.9  -30.4
3 2023-07-14 12:00:00     15.5   10.4


The spike at 14:00 on 13 July rose by over 30 °C in one hour, then dropped back again (the row after it shows the matching drop). The sun probably hit the sensor. The third row (12:00 on 14 July) is a false alarm: its “change” is large only because the previous reading was 10 hours earlier (the missing data in tab 3), so it is a real value. Always look at flagged rows before removing them.
Replace the bad value with NA rather than deleting the row, so the time series stays complete:


Code
logger_clean <- logger_clean %>%
  dplyr::mutate(air_temp = dplyr::if_else(air_temp > 40, NA_real_, air_temp)) %>%
  dplyr::select(-change)                                    # remove the helper column








Note



Choose the limits from what you know about the site and the sensor, and report them in your methods (e.g. “readings that changed by more than 5 °C within an hour were removed”). Do not remove values just because they are extreme: a real heatwave is data, not an error.




Time series can be missing data in two ways:

Blank readings (NA) in a row that exists. Count them with colSums(is.na()) as in Week 1 (section 1.2).
Missing rows: the logger recorded nothing at all, e.g. when the battery failed. These are invisible to is.na() because the rows do not exist! Find them by looking at the gap between readings, as at the top of this page.



Code
colSums(is.na(logger_clean))   # blank readings (includes the spike we removed)


date_time  air_temp 
        0         3 


Code
# Gaps longer than the 1-hour logging interval
logger_clean %>%
  dplyr::mutate(gap_hours = as.numeric(difftime(date_time, dplyr::lag(date_time), units = "hours"))) %>%
  dplyr::filter(gap_hours > 1)


# A tibble: 1 × 3
  date_time           air_temp gap_hours
  <dttm>                 <dbl>     <dbl>
1 2023-07-14 12:00:00     15.5        10


There is a 10-hour gap: 9 hourly readings are missing. tidyr::complete() adds a row, filled with NA, for every expected time, so the gaps become visible:


Code
logger_clean <- logger_clean %>%
  tidyr::complete(date_time = seq(min(date_time), max(date_time), by = "1 hour"))

nrow(logger_clean)             # 7 days x 24 hours = 168


[1] 168


Code
colSums(is.na(logger_clean))   # missing rows now show up as NA


date_time  air_temp 
        0        12 


What to do with the NAs depends on how long the gap is:

Short gaps (one or two readings) can be filled by linear interpolation: a straight line between the readings on either side. Base R’s approx() does this.
Long gaps should usually be left as NA. Interpolating across 9 hours would draw a straight line through a whole night and invent data that were never measured.



Code
# Label each run of consecutive NAs with its length
logger_clean <- logger_clean %>%
  dplyr::mutate(run_id  = cumsum(!is.na(air_temp)))      %>% # same id for an NA run
  dplyr::group_by(run_id) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(gap_length = sum(is.na(air_temp)))       %>% # length of that NA run
  dplyr::ungroup() %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    # straight-line estimate between the neighbouring readings
    interp   = approx(x = date_time, y = air_temp, xout = date_time)$y,
    # only use it for gaps of 2 readings or fewer
    air_temp_filled = dplyr::if_else(is.na(air_temp) & gap_length <= 2, interp, air_temp),
    filled   = is.na(air_temp) & !is.na(air_temp_filled)  # flag filled values
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(date_time, air_temp, air_temp_filled, filled)

sum(logger_clean$filled)       # how many values were filled


[1] 3

title: 6  OPTIONAL: Time Series
text:
Compare raw and cleaned data
Finally, compare the raw and cleaned data. Filled values are shown in red, and the long gap is left empty:


Code
raw_plot <- ggplot2::ggplot(logger_raw, ggplot2::aes(x = date_time, y = air_temp)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(colour = "grey50") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "Air temp (°C)", title = "Raw") +
  ggplot2::theme_bw()

clean_plot <- ggplot2::ggplot(logger_clean, ggplot2::aes(x = date_time, y = air_temp_filled)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line() +                                          # breaks where values are NA
  ggplot2::geom_point(data = dplyr::filter(logger_clean, filled),
                      colour = "#e12744", size = 2) +             # interpolated values
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "Air temp (°C)", title = "Cleaned") +
  ggplot2::theme_bw()

raw_plot / clean_plot















TipChecklist for raw logger data




Convert the date-time column with lubridate and plot the raw data.
Remove exact duplicate rows (dplyr::distinct(), Week 1).
Find times with more than one reading (dplyr::count(date_time)) and keep one.
Flag impossible values and sudden jumps (dplyr::lag()) and set them to NA.
Add missing times with tidyr::complete().
Interpolate only short gaps; leave long gaps as NA.
Report every cleaning step in your methods, and keep the raw file unchanged.

7  Linear and Multiple Regression

2. Visualise
Always plot the data before fitting a model. Describe the direction (positive or negative), form (linear or curved), strength (tight or scattered) and any unusual points.



What to describe when looking at a scatterplot.




Code
ggplot2::ggplot(crab_data, ggplot2::aes(x = latitude, y = size)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Latitude (°N)", y = "Carapace width (mm)") +

The relationship is positive (crabs are wider further north), roughly linear, of moderate strength, and there are no obvious errors. Notice that the points form 13 vertical stripes: every crab from the same marsh shares the same latitude. Keep that in mind for the independence assumption below.

title: 7  Linear and Multiple Regression
text:
3. Check assumptions
Fit the model first, then check the residuals with performance::check_model().


Code
# size explained by latitude
crab_lm <- lm(size ~ latitude, data = crab_data)




Code
performance::check_model(crab_lm)









Each panel has a subtitle that describes what you want to see:

The plots cannot check independence. That comes from the study design: 392 crabs were measured, but they come from only 13 marshes, and crabs from the same marsh share the same environment. This means we have less independent information than 392 data points suggest, and the p-value will be too small. We will handle this properly with a mixed-effects model in Week 12. For now we note it as a caveat.
Influential points deserve a closer look. Use the app to see how a single point can change the regression line, depending on where it sits.


App: leverage and influential points





Code
viewof inf_x = Inputs.range([-10, 50], {value: 42, step: 1, label: "Red point: x position"})
viewof inf_y = Inputs.range([-20, 60], {value: 5, step: 1, label: "Red point: y position"})
viewof inf_n = Inputs.range([5, 60], {value: 20, step: 1, label: "Number of black points"})
viewof inf_seed = Inputs.button("Resample")


































Code
inf_data = {
  const r = rng(808 + inf_seed);
  const n = inf_n;
  const xb = Array.from({length: n}, (_, i) => (i * 20) / (n - 1));
  const yb = xb.map((v) => v + rnorm(r, 1, 0, 3)[0]);
  const x = [...xb, inf_x], y = [...yb, inf_y];
  const all = lm1(x, y), black = lm1(xb, yb);
  const pts = x.map((v, i) => ({x: v, y: y[i], red: i === n, hat: all.hat[i], std: all.stdres[i], cook: all.cook[i]}));
  return {pts, all, black, n};
}

inf_scatter = Plot.plot({
  width: 330, height: 260, marginLeft: 40,
  x: {domain: [-12, 52], label: "x"}, y: {domain: [-25, 65], label: "y", grid: true},

    Plot.dot(inf_data.pts.filter((d) => !d.red), {x: "x", y: "y", fill: dark, r: 3}),
    Plot.dot(inf_data.pts.filter((d) => d.red), {x: "x", y: "y", fill: red, r: 7, symbol: "triangle"})
  ]
})

inf_lev = Plot.plot({

  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX([2 * 2 / (inf_data.n + 1)], {stroke: red, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: grey}),
    Plot.dot(inf_data.pts.filter((d) => !d.red), {x: "hat", y: "std", fill: dark, r: 3}),

})

html`<div><div class="app-row"><div><div class="app-plot-label">Data and fitted lines</div>${inf_scatter}</div><div><div class="app-plot-label">Residuals vs leverage</div>${inf_lev}</div></div>

${inf_red.cook > 1 ? "This point is <b>highly influential</b>: it changes the slope on its own."
  : inf_red.hat > 4 / (inf_data.n + 1) ? "High leverage (unusual x) but the point follows the trend, so it has little influence."
  : "This point has little influence on the fitted line."}
Move the red point far to the right <i>and</i> away from the trend to make it influential.</div></div>`








































Leverage measures how unusual a point’s x value is. Cook’s distance combines leverage with the size of the residual. A point is only a problem when it is both unusual in x and far from the line. Never delete a point just because it is influential. Check whether it is a data entry error (Week 1) and, if it is real, report the results with and without it.

The fitted model is:
\[

\]

Slope (0.485): carapace width increases by about 0.49 mm for every degree further north (95% CI 0.42–0.55 mm). Across the 12 degrees sampled, that is about 5.8 mm.

Before we start
Week 8: Modelling counts with Poisson and negative binomial GLMs
Much of ecology is counting: the number of birds on a transect, seedlings in a quadrat, frogs calling at a pond. title: 8  Generalised Linear Models: Count Data
text:
1. Background

Why not use lm() for counts?







Property of counts
Problem for a linear model




Whole numbers ≥ 0
A straight line can predict negative counts


Often skewed with many small values and a few large ones
Residuals are not normal


Variance increases with the mean
Breaks the equal-variance assumption



Transforming counts (e.g. log(y + 1)) is an old fix that often works poorly, especially when there are many zeros. A GLM models the counts directly.


The two ingredients of a GLM

A distribution for the response. For counts, the starting point is the Poisson distribution, which describes the number of random events in a fixed amount of space or time.
A link function that connects the predictors to the mean. For counts this is the log link:

\[
\log(\mu_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mu_i = e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i}
\]
The model is a straight line on the log scale, which becomes an exponential curve on the count scale, and the predicted mean (\(\mu\)) can never be negative. Because of the log, coefficients are multiplicative: \(e^{\beta_1}\) is the factor by which the expected count changes for every one-unit increase in x. This is called the rate ratio.


Overdispersion
The Poisson distribution makes a strong assumption: the variance equals the mean. Ecological counts are usually more variable than that, because animals cluster, habitats are patchy and there are factors we did not measure. This is overdispersion. If you ignore it, standard errors are too small and p-values too optimistic. The usual fix is the negative binomial distribution, which has an extra parameter (k, or theta in R) that allows the variance to be larger than the mean.
Use the app to compare Poisson counts with overdispersed (negative binomial) counts that have the same mean.


App: Poisson versus overdispersed counts





Code
import {rng, rpois1, rnbinom1, mean, variance, fmt, red, grey, dark} from "./apps/ecs200.js"









Code
viewof ct_mu = Inputs.range([0.5, 20], {value: 4, step: 0.5, label: "Mean count per sample"})
viewof ct_k = Inputs.range([0.3, 50], {value: 50, step: 0.1, label: "Clumping parameter k (small = more overdispersed)"})
viewof ct_seed = Inputs.button("Resample 300 samples")



























Code
ct_data = {
  const r = rng(301 + ct_seed);
  const counts = Array.from({length: 300}, () => (ct_k >= 50 ? rpois1(r, ct_mu) : rnbinom1(r, ct_mu, ct_k)));
  const maxc = Math.max(...counts, Math.ceil(ct_mu * 2.5));
  // expected Poisson frequencies with the same mean
  const pois = [];
  let p = Math.exp(-ct_mu);
  for (let c = 0; c <= maxc; c++) { pois.push({count: c, expected: 300 * p}); p = p * ct_mu / (c + 1); }
  return {counts, pois};
}

Plot.plot({
  width: 560, height: 280, marginLeft: 45,
  x: {label: "Count in a sample", round: true}, y: {label: "Number of samples", grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.rectY(ct_data.counts, Plot.binX({y: "count"}, {x: (d) => d, interval: 1, fill: grey, inset: 0.5})),
    Plot.line(ct_data.pois, {x: (d) => d.count + 0.5, y: "expected", stroke: red, strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.dot(ct_data.pois, {x: (d) => d.count + 0.5, y: "expected", fill: red, r: 3.5}),
    Plot.ruleY([0])
  ]
})

variance / mean = <b>${fmt(variance(ct_data.counts) / mean(ct_data.counts))}</b> (a Poisson distribution gives about 1).
Zeros: <b>${ct_data.counts.filter((d) => d === 0).length}</b> observed vs <b>${fmt(ct_data.pois[0].expected, 0)}</b> expected under Poisson.
${ct_k >= 50 ? "These counts are Poisson: the grey bars follow the red line (the Poisson expectation)."
  : "These counts are overdispersed: there are more zeros and more very large counts than a Poisson distribution (red line) expects."}</div>`


















NoteIs a zero really a zero?



Before modelling counts, think about what your zeros mean. A zero can be a true zero (the species really was absent, or was present but by chance was not in the sample) or a false zero (the species was there but you missed it, e.g. a sampling design or observer error). False zeros should be avoided through good design rather than fixed by the model (Blasco-Moreno et al., 2019). See Research Design for examples.

title: 8  Generalised Linear Models: Count Data
text:
3. Check assumptions
GLMs do not assume normal residuals or equal variances. The key assumptions are:







Assumption
How to check




The chosen distribution fits the data (no overdispersion for Poisson)
performance::check_overdispersion() for a Poisson model; the posterior predictive check in performance::check_model()


No more zeros than the distribution expects
Compare observed and predicted zeros (see below)


The relationship is linear on the log (link) scale
Plot the data; performance::check_model()


Independent observations
Study design: one sample per stream ✅. Repeated samples from the same stream would need a mixed-effects model (Week 12)



Step 1: start with a Poisson GLM. Use glm() with family = poisson. The log link is the default for Poisson.


Code
mayfly_pois <- glm(mayflies ~ canopy_cover + land_use,
                   family = poisson,
                   data = mayfly_data)

# Is the variance bigger than the Poisson model expects?
performance::check_overdispersion(mayfly_pois)


# Overdispersion test

       dispersion ratio =   4.291
  Pearson's Chi-Squared = 244.583
                p-value = < 0.001


The dispersion ratio should be close to 1. A ratio well above 1 with a small p-value means the data are overdispersed, so the Poisson model is not appropriate.
Step 2: switch to a negative binomial GLM. MASS::glm.nb() works like glm(), uses the log link and estimates the extra dispersion parameter (theta) for you.


Code
mayfly_nb <- MASS::glm.nb(mayflies ~ canopy_cover + land_use,
                          data = mayfly_data)

performance::check_model(mayfly_nb)









Then compare the number of zeros in the data with the number the model expects. dnbinom(0, ...) gives each stream’s predicted probability of a zero count, and adding these up gives the expected number of zeros.


Code
# Observed number of streams with no mayflies
sum(mayfly_data$mayflies == 0)


[1] 4


Code
# Number of zeros expected by the negative binomial model
sum(dnbinom(0, mu = fitted(mayfly_nb), size = mayfly_nb$theta))


[1] 3.381428


In the posterior predictive check, the data simulated from the model (blue) now look like the real data (green), the other panels look reasonable, and the model predicts about as many zeros as were observed. The negative binomial model is appropriate.






NoteReading check_model() for a GLM (click to expand)





For GLMs, the residuals are not expected to be normal, so check_model() shows slightly different panels. It uses simulated residuals for the “uniformity” or “normality” panels and adds a posterior predictive check: the model is used to simulate many new datasets (blue lines), which should look like your real data (green line). If the simulated data have far fewer zeros or a much narrower spread than the real data, the distribution is wrong.









WarningWhen are these models NOT appropriate? (click to expand)












What you see
What to do




Dispersion ratio > 1 in a Poisson GLM
Negative binomial GLM, MASS::glm.nb() (this workshop)


Many more zeros than even the negative binomial predicts
Zero-inflated or hurdle models (e.g. glmmTMB package). Think first about whether the zeros are true or false (Blasco-Moreno et al., 2019)


Samples differ in effort (different trap nights, transect lengths or areas)
Add an offset: glm(count ~ x + offset(log(effort)), family = poisson). The model then describes counts per unit of effort


Counts out of a known total (e.g. 7 of 20 seeds germinated)
Binomial GLM (Week 11)


Several samples from the same site, plot or individual
Generalised linear mixed model (lme4::glmer(), Week 12)


Very large counts with no zeros and a symmetrical spread
An lm() may be fine. Check the residuals

title: 8  Generalised Linear Models: Count Data
text:
4. Model


Code
summary(mayfly_nb)



Call:
MASS::glm.nb(formula = mayflies ~ canopy_cover + land_use, data = mayfly_data, 
    init.theta = 3.517850702, link = log)

Coefficients:
                     Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)          1.271614   0.323195   3.935 8.34e-05 ***
canopy_cover         0.026562   0.004609   5.764 8.24e-09 ***
land_useagriculture -0.758751   0.239911  -3.163  0.00156 ** 
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for Negative Binomial(3.5179) family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 209.769  on 59  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance:  67.222  on 57  degrees of freedom
AIC: 370.06

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 1

              Theta:  3.518 
          Std. Err.:  0.965 

 2 x log-likelihood:  -362.062 


The output gives everything you need:

Coefficients: one row per term.

Estimate: the effect on the log scale. (Intercept) is the log of the expected count for a forest stream with 0% canopy cover (the reference level). canopy_cover is the change in log(count) for each 1% more cover. land_useagriculture is the difference in log(count) between agricultural and forest streams at the same canopy cover. A positive estimate means more mayflies, a negative one fewer.
Std. Error: the uncertainty in each estimate.
z value: the estimate divided by its standard error (GLMs use z instead of t).
Pr(>|z|): the p-value, the probability of an effect this large if the true effect were zero.

Dispersion parameter for Negative Binomial(...) family: the estimated theta (k). Small values mean strongly clumped counts; very large values mean the counts are close to Poisson.
Null deviance and Residual deviance: how badly a model with no predictors and our model fit the data. The bigger the drop, the more the predictors explain.
AIC: a measure of fit that penalises extra parameters, used to compare models fitted to the same data (lower is better).
Theta and Std. Err.: theta again, with its standard error.

The coefficients are on the log scale. Back-transform them with exp() to get rate ratios, which are much easier to interpret.


Code
# Rate ratios and their 95% confidence intervals
exp(coef(mayfly_nb))


        (Intercept)        canopy_cover land_useagriculture 
          3.5666038           1.0269176           0.4682508 


Code
exp(confint(mayfly_nb))


                        2.5 %    97.5 %
(Intercept)         1.8630870 6.8868545
canopy_cover        1.0174457 1.0366409
land_useagriculture 0.2890159 0.7552373


Plot the model’s predictions on the count scale.


Code
# Predicted counts across canopy cover for each land use (with 95% CIs)
mayfly_pred <- ggeffects::predict_response(mayfly_nb, terms = c("canopy_cover", "land_use"))

plot(mayfly_pred, show_data = TRUE) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c("darkgreen", "#e12744")) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = c("darkgreen", "#e12744")) +
  ggplot2::labs(title = NULL, x = "Canopy cover (%)", y = "Mayfly nymphs per sample",
                colour = "Land use", fill = "Land use")









The prediction lines curve upwards because the model is linear on the log scale.

title: 8  Generalised Linear Models: Count Data
text:
5. Interpret









Term
Rate ratio
95% CI
Meaning




canopy_cover
1.027
1.017–1.037
Each 1% increase in canopy cover multiplies the expected count by 1.027, i.e. 3% more mayflies. Over 10% more cover that is ×1.3


land_useagriculture
0.47
0.29–0.76
At the same canopy cover, agricultural streams have 0.47 times as many mayflies as forest streams, i.e. 53% fewer



A rate ratio of 1 means no effect. If the 95% CI of a rate ratio does not include 1, the effect is significant at α = 0.05.
Methods sentence: Mayfly counts were analysed with a negative binomial generalised linear model (log link) with canopy cover and land use as predictors, fitted with MASS::glm.nb() in R. A Poisson model was rejected because the counts were overdispersed (dispersion ratio = 4.3). Significance was set at α = 0.05.
Results sentence:

Mayfly abundance increased with riparian canopy cover, by 3% for every 1% increase in cover (rate ratio = 1.027, 95% CI 1.017–1.037, p < 0.001). At the same canopy cover, streams in agricultural catchments had 53% fewer mayflies than forested streams (rate ratio = 0.47, 95% CI 0.29–0.76, p = 0.002; Fig. 1).

title: 9  OPTIONAL: Spatial Data
text:
Download the data
Week 9 (study week): Downloading and mapping species occurrence data
This is an optional tutorial for anyone working with species occurrence or other spatial data.
Maps are one of the most useful tools an ecologist has. A quick map of species observations shows where a species has been recorded, the extent of your data, and possible errors (e.g. a frog recorded in the ocean). In this tutorial you will download records of the motorbike frog (Litoria moorei) in Western Australia since 2000 from FrogID, and map them.

Coordinate reference systems
The Earth is round but maps are flat, so every map uses a coordinate reference system (CRS) to flatten it. Our WA outline uses GDA94:


Code
sf::st_crs(wa_map)$input


[1] "EPSG:4283"


The same outline looks different in different CRSs. sf::st_transform() changes the CRS:


Code
crs_gda94 <- ggplot2::ggplot(wa_map) +
  ggplot2::geom_sf(colour = "grey60", fill = "#F5F5F5") +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "GDA94") +
  ggplot2::theme_bw()

crs_wa <- wa_map %>%
  sf::st_transform(crs = 7850) %>%   # a projection designed for WA (GDA2020 / MGA zone 50)

  ggplot2::geom_sf(colour = "grey60", fill = "#F5F5F5") +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "EPSG:7850") +

crs_canada <- wa_map %>%
  sf::st_transform(crs = 2955) %>%   # a projection designed for Canada!

title: 10  OPTIONAL: Movement Data
text:
Tracking technologies
Week 10: Cleaning and plotting animal tracking data
This is an optional tutorial for anyone working with animal tracking (telemetry) data.
Tracking data combine location and time, so this tutorial builds on the optional time series and spatial data tutorials.
How do we track animals in the wild? There are many methods, and how you process, analyse and interpret movement data depends heavily on the method used.

title: 10  OPTIONAL: Movement Data
text:
Load all the GPS files
Each bird has its own file. list.files() finds them, and purrr::map() imports each one with readr::read_csv(), then purrr::list_rbind() stacks them into one data frame. id = "file_name" adds a column with the name of the file each row came from. We read Date and Time as text because the files use different date formats.


Code
# Find every file in the gps_study folder that starts with "GV" and ends in .csv
gps_files <- list.files(path = "data/gps_study", pattern = "^GV.*\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)

Merge with metadata
The metadata file holds one row per tag deployment: the bird ID, when the tag was attached and removed, and the nest location. These times were recorded in local time (Indian/Chagos), so we convert them to GMT to match the GPS data.

  dplyr::mutate(
    ID          = BirdID,
    deploy_time = lubridate::dmy_hms(paste(DeploymentDate, DeploymentTime), tz = "Indian/Chagos"),
    deploy_time = lubridate::with_tz(deploy_time, tzone = "GMT"),   # local time to GMT
    nest_lon    = NestLong,
    nest_lat    = NestLat) %>%
  dplyr::select(ID, Population, BreedingStage, deploy_time, nest_lon, nest_lat)

gps_merged <- gps_merged %>%

title: 10  OPTIONAL: Movement Data
text:
Movement metrics
To find impossible fixes, calculate for each fix (within each bird):

the distance from the previous fix,
the time since the previous fix,
the speed (distance / time),
the net displacement: the distance from the first fix (the nest).

geosphere::distHaversine() calculates the distance in metres between two sets of longitude/latitude points, allowing for the curvature of the Earth. dplyr::lag() gives the previous value, and dplyr::first() the first value.


Code
gps_metrics <- gps_merged %>%
  dplyr::group_by(ID) %>%                                       # calculate within each bird
  dplyr::mutate(
    dist_m     = geosphere::distHaversine(cbind(lon, lat), cbind(dplyr::lag(lon), dplyr::lag(lat))),
    time_s     = as.numeric(difftime(date_time, dplyr::lag(date_time), units = "secs")),
    speed_ms   = dist_m / time_s,                               # metres per second
    netdisp_km = geosphere::distHaversine(cbind(lon, lat), cbind(dplyr::first(lon), dplyr::first(lat))) / 1000) %>%
  dplyr::ungroup()

  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ ID) +

  ggplot2::geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Speed (m/s)", y = "Count") +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ ID) +
  ggplot2::theme_bw()

  ggplot2::geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Net displacement from first fix (km)", y = "Count") +

title: 10  OPTIONAL: Movement Data
text:
Filter out errors
Choose thresholds from the biology of your species (and the literature), then filter:

Deployment period: remove the first 30 minutes after the tag was attached, when the bird may behave unnaturally after handling.
Speed: red-footed boobies rarely fly faster than about 20 m/s, so faster “movements” are GPS errors.
Net displacement: these birds were rearing chicks and returning to the nest, so fixes more than 300 km away are errors.

If your GPS data have a dilution of precision (DOP) column, you can also remove fixes with poor precision (e.g. DOP > 8).


Code
gps_clean <- gps_metrics %>%
  dplyr::filter(date_time > deploy_time + lubridate::minutes(30), # after the first 30 min
                is.na(speed_ms) | speed_ms < 20,                 # keep the first fix (no speed) and realistic speeds
                netdisp_km <= 300)                               # within 300 km of the start

# How many fixes were removed for each bird?
dplyr::left_join(dplyr::count(gps_metrics, ID, name = "before"),
                 dplyr::count(gps_clean, ID, name = "after"),
                 by = "ID")

Before we start
Week 11: Logistic regression for presence/absence, alive/dead and other yes/no responses
Many ecological questions have a yes/no answer. Is the species present at this site? Did the seedling survive? Did the coral bleach? Did the bird nest successfully? title: 11  Generalised Linear Models: Binary Data
text:
3. Check assumptions
Residuals from binary data are always strange-looking (every residual comes from a 0 or a 1), so the usual residual plots are not useful. Instead:



Assumption
How to check




Independent observations
Study design: one survey per dam ✅. Repeated surveys of the same dam would need a mixed-effects model (Week 12)


The relationship is linear on the logit scale
Binned residuals: group observations by their fitted value and average the residuals in each bin. Most bins should fall inside the error bounds


Enough data
A rough rule is at least 10 observations of the rarer outcome (0 or 1) for every predictor. Here both outcomes have more than 40 dams, and there are only 2 predictors ✅


Predictors are not strongly correlated
performance::check_collinearity()



Overdispersion cannot happen with 0/1 data, so there is nothing to check for it.


Code
frog_glm <- glm(frog_present ~ veg_cover + fish,
                family = binomial,
                data = frog_data)

# Binned residuals: points should mostly fall inside the grey bounds
plot(performance::binned_residuals(frog_glm))











Code
# All diagnostics together
performance::check_model(frog_glm)









The binned residuals fall inside the bounds and the collinearity is low, so the model is appropriate.






WarningWhen is logistic regression NOT appropriate, or not enough? (click to expand)












Situation
What to do




Imperfect detection: a single survey can miss a species that is really there (a false absence)
Survey each site several times and use an occupancy model, which estimates detection and occupancy separately (Specht et al., 2017). Logistic regression then models “detected”, not “present”


Successes out of a known number of trials (e.g. 7 of 20 eggs hatched)
Binomial GLM with cbind(successes, failures) ~ x as the response


A continuous proportion (e.g. % cover)
Beta regression (e.g. glmmTMB package with family = beta_family())


Repeated surveys at the same sites, or sites grouped in regions
Mixed model, lme4::glmer(..., family = binomial) (Week 12)


Warning “fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred”
Complete separation: a predictor perfectly predicts the outcome (e.g. all dams with fish have no frogs). Estimates are unreliable, so collect more data or simplify the model


A time until the event happens (e.g. days until death)
Survival analysis (Week 13)

text:
4. Model


Code
summary(frog_glm)



Call:
glm(formula = frog_present ~ veg_cover + fish, family = binomial, 
    data = frog_data)

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept) -1.53941    0.56548  -2.722  0.00648 ** 
veg_cover    0.03970    0.01015   3.910 9.21e-05 ***
fishpresent -1.70076    0.54490  -3.121  0.00180 ** 
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 124.589  on 89  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance:  96.466  on 87  degrees of freedom
AIC: 102.47

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 4


The output gives everything you need:

Coefficients: one row per term.

Estimate: the effect on the log-odds scale. (Intercept) is the log-odds of detecting frogs at a dam with 0% vegetation and no fish (the reference level). veg_cover is the change in log-odds for each 1% more vegetated shoreline. fishpresent is the difference in log-odds between dams with and without fish. A positive estimate means frogs are more likely to be detected, a negative one less likely.
Std. Error: the uncertainty in each estimate.
z value: the estimate divided by its standard error.
Pr(>|z|): the p-value, the probability of an effect this large if the true effect were zero.

Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1: fixed at 1 for 0/1 data, which is why there is no overdispersion to check.
Null deviance and Residual deviance: how badly a model with no predictors and our model fit the data. The bigger the drop, the more the predictors explain.
AIC: compares models fitted to the same data (lower is better).
Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: how many steps R took to fit the model. You can ignore it unless it is very large (over about 25), which can be a sign of complete separation.

As in Week 8, the coefficients are on the link scale (here log-odds). Back-transform them with exp() to get odds ratios.

exp(coef(frog_glm))     # odds ratios


(Intercept)   veg_cover fishpresent

fishpresent 0.05866736 0.5068468

                y = "Probability of detecting frogs", colour = "Fish", fill = "Fish")

title: 11  Generalised Linear Models: Binary Data
text:
5. Interpret









Term
Odds ratio
95% CI
Meaning




veg_cover
1.04
1.021–1.063
Each extra 1% of vegetated shoreline multiplies the odds of detecting frogs by 1.04. For a 10% increase: ×1.49


fishpresent
0.18
0.06–0.51
With fish present, the odds of detecting frogs are 0.18 times the odds without fish, i.e. the odds are reduced by 82%









ImportantOdds are not probabilities



An odds ratio of 0.2 does not mean the probability is 80% lower. The change in probability depends on where you are on the S-curve. That is why it is good practice to also report predicted probabilities, as in the results sentence below.


Methods sentence: Frog detection (detected/not detected) was modelled with a binomial generalised linear model (logistic regression) using the glm() function in R, with fringing vegetation cover and fish presence as predictors. Model fit was assessed with binned residuals using the performance::binned_residuals() function. Significance was set at α = 0.05.
Results sentence:

The probability of detecting frogs increased with fringing vegetation (odds ratio = 1.04 per 1% cover, 95% CI 1.021–1.063, p < 0.001) and was lower at dams with fish (odds ratio = 0.18, 95% CI 0.06–0.51, p < 0.001; Fig. 1). At dams without fish, the predicted probability of detecting frogs rose from 0.24 at 10% vegetation cover to 0.88 at 90% cover, whereas at dams with fish it rose from 0.06 to 0.58. Because each dam was surveyed once, these are probabilities of detection, which may underestimate true occupancy.

title: 12  Mixed-Effects Models
text:
Before we start
Week 12: Accounting for sites, repeated measurements and other sampling structure with random effects
So far, every model has assumed that each observation is independent. In real ecological studies (including your project) that is rarely true: we measure the same animal more than once, take several quadrats from each site, or put several seedlings in each pot.
This week you will learn mixed-effects models, which add random effects to a linear model to account for this structure. Workshop materials are available in the GitHub repository ECS200.
lizard_repeated.csv  pie_crab.csv
We need two new packages. lme4 fits mixed models, and lmerTest is a small add-on that gives lme4 models p-values.

title: 12  Mixed-Effects Models
text:
Study context
In Week 5 every lizard was raced only once. That needs a lot of lizards. A more efficient design is to race the same lizard at several temperatures. Here, 16 dragons were each raced at 18, 22, 26 and 30 °C (in random order, with a rest day between trials), giving 64 sprint speeds.

2. Visualise
Plot each lizard as its own line (“spaghetti plot”). This shows the grouping structure immediately.


Code
ggplot2::ggplot(lizard_rm, ggplot2::aes(x = temperature, y = sprint_speed, group = lizard_id)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(alpha = 0.5) +   # one line per lizard

title: 12  Mixed-Effects Models
text:
3. Check assumptions
A linear mixed model has the same assumptions as a linear model (linearity, equal variance and normal residuals) plus one more: the random effects are normally distributed. The independence assumption now only applies after accounting for the grouping.


Code
# Random intercept model
lizard_lmm <- lmerTest::lmer(sprint_speed ~ temperature + (1 | lizard_id),
                             data = lizard_rm)

performance::check_model(lizard_lmm)

















Assumption
Panel
Here




Linearity
Linearity
✅ Flat reference line


Equal variance
Homogeneity of variance
✅


Normal residuals
Normality of residuals
✅


Normal random effects
Normality of random effects (lizard_id)
✅ Dots close to the line


Independence, given the grouping
Study design
✅ Lizards are different animals, tested in random order









WarningWhen do you need something different? (click to expand)












Situation
What to do




Groups differ in their slope as well as their intercept (the spaghetti lines are not parallel)
Add a random slope: (1 + temperature \| lizard_id). This needs plenty of data per group


Groups within groups, e.g. quadrats within sites within regions
Nested random effects: (1 \| region/site)


Two separate groupings, e.g. site and year
Crossed random effects: (1 \| site) + (1 \| year)


Counts or binary responses with grouping
Generalised linear mixed model: lme4::glmer(count ~ x + (1 \| site), family = poisson)


Fewer than about 5 groups
Fit the grouping as a fixed effect, e.g. lm(y ~ x + site)


Message boundary (singular) fit
The random effect variance is estimated as zero, often because there are too few groups or little variation among them. Check the data. The model may not need that random effect


Measurements close in time are more similar than distant ones
Temporal autocorrelation (see the optional Week 6 on time series)

The output gives everything you need:

Linear mixed model fit by REML: REML (restricted maximum likelihood) is the default fitting method. t-tests use Satterthwaite's method means lmerTest calculated the degrees of freedom and p-values.
Scaled residuals: a quick summary of the residuals. The median should be near 0 and the minimum and maximum roughly symmetrical.
Random effects: how the unexplained variation is split.

lizard_id (Intercept): the Variance and Std.Dev. of the baseline speeds between lizards. A large value means lizards differ a lot.
Residual: the variation within a lizard, left over after temperature and lizard identity.

Number of obs: 64, groups: lizard_id, 16: check these match your design (16 lizards × 4 temperatures).
Fixed effects: interpreted exactly like lm().

Estimate: (Intercept) is the predicted speed of the average lizard at 0 °C (outside the data, so not meaningful on its own). temperature is the change in sprint speed per °C for the average lizard.
Std. Error: the uncertainty in each estimate, now accounting for the repeated measures.
df: degrees of freedom from Satterthwaite’s method (usually a decimal).
t value and Pr(>|t|): the test statistic and p-value.

Correlation of Fixed Effects: how strongly the estimates are related to each other. You can usually ignore it.

title: 12  Mixed-Effects Models
text:
5. Interpret

Temperature: sprint speed increased by 0.044 m/s per °C (95% CI 0.039–0.049), i.e. about 0.53 m/s across the 12 °C range tested.
Random effects: lizards differed in their baseline speed with an SD of 0.31 m/s, while the residual SD within a lizard was 0.09 m/s. The ICC of 0.92 means 92% of the unexplained variation was due to consistent differences between individual lizards.
R2: temperature alone explains 0.28 of the variation (marginal R2), and temperature plus lizard identity explain 0.94 (conditional R2).

Methods sentence: Because each lizard was tested at all four temperatures, the effect of temperature on sprint speed was analysed with a linear mixed-effects model with temperature as a fixed effect and lizard identity as a random intercept, fitted with lme4 and lmerTest in R (p-values from Satterthwaite’s degrees of freedom). Significance was set at α = 0.05.
Results sentence:

Sprint speed increased with temperature by 0.044 m/s per °C (95% CI 0.039–0.049; t47 = 17.3, p < 0.001; Fig. 1). Individual lizards differed consistently in speed (SD among lizards = 0.31 m/s; ICC = 0.92).

title: 13  Survival Analysis
text:
Before we start
Week 13: Time-to-event data, censoring, Kaplan–Meier curves and Cox models
How long does a translocated animal survive? How many days until a seed germinates, a plant flowers, or an insect is knocked down by heat? These are time-to-event questions. They need their own methods, because in almost every study some individuals have not had the event by the time the study ends.
This week you will learn survival analysis, which handles this properly. Workshop materials are available in the GitHub repository ECS200.
woylie_survival.csv
We use survival, which comes installed with R, for the models, and ggsurvfit to draw survival curves with ggplot2.

title: 13  Survival Analysis
text:
Study context



Woylie or brush-tailed bettong (Bettongia ogilbyi) illustration by H. C. Richter in Gould’s Mammals of Australia, 1863.


The woylie (brush-tailed bettong, Bettongia ogilbyi) is a critically endangered marsupial from south-west Western Australia. Predation by introduced foxes and cats is a major threat, so woylies are often translocated into predator-proof fenced reserves. Translocations outside fences can establish wider populations, but only if enough animals survive.
Sixty woylies were radio-collared and released, 30 inside a fenced reserve and 30 in an unfenced reserve with predator baiting. Each animal was tracked for up to 365 days. For each woylie, the data record:

days: days from release until death, or until tracking stopped;
status: 1 = the woylie died during the study; 0 = the woylie was still alive when tracking stopped (the study ended, or its collar failed);
release_site (fenced or unfenced) and body mass at release (mass_g).

Question: Does survival differ between fenced and unfenced release sites?


Code
woylie_data <- readr::read_csv("data/woylie_survival.csv") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(release_site = factor(release_site, levels = c("fenced", "unfenced")))

3. Check assumptions







Assumption
How to check




Independent (non-informative) censoring: whether an animal is censored has nothing to do with its risk of dying
Study design. A collar failing at random is fine. Losing track of animals because they were dying (e.g. collar destroyed by a predator but recorded as “lost”) is not

Study design

The output gives everything you need:

The first table has one row per predictor:

coef: the effect on the log-hazard scale. Positive means a higher risk of death, negative a lower risk. release_siteunfenced compares unfenced with fenced (the reference level); mass_g is per gram of body mass.
exp(coef): the hazard ratio. Above 1 = higher risk, below 1 = lower risk, 1 = no effect.
se(coef): the standard error of coef.
z and Pr(>|z|): the test statistic and p-value for each predictor.

Concordance: how well the model ranks which animals died first (0.5 = no better than chance, 1 = perfect).
Likelihood ratio test, Wald test and Score (logrank) test: three versions of an overall test of whether the predictors together explain survival. They usually agree; report the predictor-level results above.

Methods sentence: Survival of radio-collared woylies was estimated with the Kaplan–Meier method (ggsurvfit::survfit2()) and compared between release sites with a log-rank test (survival::survdiff()) in R. The effects of release site and body mass on the risk of death were estimated with a Cox proportional hazards model, using the survival::coxph() function from the survival package in R. Animals alive at the end of the 365-day study or whose collars failed were treated as censored. The proportional hazards assumption was checked with Schoenfeld residuals (cox.zph()). Significance was set at α = 0.05.
Results sentence:

Survival over the first year was much higher inside the fenced reserve (71% surviving at 365 days) than at the unfenced site (0%; median survival = 95 days; log-rank χ²1 = 44, p < 0.001; Fig. 1). After accounting for body mass, woylies released outside the fence had 17.8 times the hazard of death (95% CI 5.8–54.6, p < 0.001). There was no clear effect of body mass on the risk of death (HR per 100 g = 0.88, 95% CI 0.69–1.13, p = 0.31).
